newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Horsetrading starts in earnest on EU enlargement.
newsitem.headline: Horsetrading starts in earnest on EU enlargement.

text.p: A fortnight before the European Commission unveils its assessments on how suitable 10 former Iron Curtain countries are for EU membership, horsetrading has begun in earnest to decide who will cross the threshold first.

Draft factual documents assessing each of the Eastern Europeans' preparedness in areas ranging from the application of EU single market legislation, through farming, to political reforms are already starting to circulate at the EU executive.

But the page that matters -- saying whether membership talks should be opened and when -- remains blank and will do so until shortly before the Commission reaches a final decision on July 15, Commission officials told Reuters.
"It is all changing from minute to minute. Nobody has seen any concluding papers," one Commission official said. "There's going to be some horsetrading."

Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary, Slovenia, Slovakia, Estonia, Latvia, Lithuania, Romania and Bulgaria are all in the line for EU membership and it is up to EU governments to decide whether talks should open with all of them at once or to stagger them.

But, despite EU assurances to the 10 last week that the enlargement will not fall victim to an internal EU power struggle, the Commission is aware that EU leaders have dug the enlargement plan into a hole by failing to agree on the necessary institutional reforms at their June 16-17 summit.

The leaders, meeting in Amsterdam, agreed that only if the EU expanded beyond 20 members would it be necessary to hold another inter-governmental conference to overhaul the internal EU power balance, currently framed for its 15 members.

That means, Commission officials say, that at least psychologically the Commission has in mind that it must either limit the first enlargement wave to five, or risk seeing the expansion delayed by a new EU conference.
So the question is -- if only five can enter, who should be left out?

Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary have been widely considered as the frontrunners, even though the European Commission has regularly cited discontent with Poland's economic performance and the speed with which it takes on EU law.
Estonia and Slovenia are also seen as advanced enough -- making five. So where is the problem?
The situation is complicated by the fact that Cyprus, already judged by the European Commission to fit the bill for membership, has already been waiting in the queue for some time.

The Mediterranean island's foreign minister Yiannakis Cassoulides told reporters last week in Amsterdam that he was confident EU member Greece would not allow Cyprus to be left out of the first EU expansion.
Cyprus argues that EU membership would vastly facilitate UN- brokered talks to find a solution to the divided island.
So if Poland, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Cyprus have to be in, and the expansion has to be limited to five, who will be left out -- Estonia or Slovenia? And is it possible?
Some EU officials say if one goes in, so must the other.

Faced with this quandary different Commissioners are engaged in heavy lobbying with those from the nordic countries pushing the case of the Baltic states, and Estonia in particular, while those from the south push Slovenia.

The two countries' case is made more urgent by the fact that both will almost certainly be left out of the first enlargement wave of the NATO military alliance, which is expected to limit its first expansion wave to Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary at its July 8-9 summit in Madrid.

The EU says there is no link between its own plans and those of NATO, but the countries themselves have warned of the impact back home of a double rejection when they are trying to distance themselves from their ex-Soviet past, in the case of Estonia, and an ex-Yugoslav past, in the case of Slovenia.
